raw_case_text:
A 79-year-old man with hypertension and chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) presented with dysphasia after the first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody). He was initially diagnosed with CLL a year earlier and initiated therapy due to fatigue and progressive anemia (hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL) without prior infections. His baseline absolute neutrophil count was 2.7 x 109/L, absolute lymphocyte count was 16.3 x 109/L, absolute monocyte count was 0.3 x 109/L, and IgG level obtained at diagnosis was 805 mg/dL. There was no history of use of corticosteroids or other immunosuppressive medications. He used to work in construction but had retired many years prior and had remained very active in his garden until initiation of chemotherapy. There was no other pertinent medical, surgical, social, or family history. Except for slurred speech, his physical exam was unremarkable. Brain MRI showed 3 distinct left temporal and parietal lobe abscesses with significant edema (Figure 1), for which he was started on high-dose dexamethasone 4 mg four times daily. Chest CT revealed a pulmonary nodule (Figure 2). Blood cultures, serum cryptococcal Ag, Aspergillus Ag (galactomannan, using the Platelia Aspergillus enzyme immunoassay (EIA)), and beta-D-glucan (betaDg) were negative. Stereotactic brain biopsy of one of the abscesses failed to include its necrotic core and was nondiagnostic. Plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing (cfDNA NGS) showed a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus. Therefore, the patient was discharged on dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, ceftriaxone, minocycline, and linezolid, which was subsequently discontinued because of thrombocytopenia.
Repeat imaging revealed decrease in the size of the brain abscesses (Figure 1) and of the pulmonary nodule with central cavitation (Figure 2). However, he had recurrence of dysphasia and brain edema on imaging soon after tapering and discontinuation of dexamethasone approximately 6 weeks from initial presentation. He was restarted on dexamethasone 4 mg twice daily, with a plan for a slower taper.
After two more weeks, approximately two months from his initial presentation, he was admitted to the intensive care unit with multiorgan (respiratory, renal, and heart) failure. Brain MRI showed significant decrease in the size of previous abscesses, but also many new infarcts (Figure 1). Chest CT showed multiple lung masses with cavitation, consistent with new abscesses (Figure 3). Repeat betaDg was negative, but galactomannan was >9.3 (EIA assay cut-off). His family opted for comfort measures only, and kindly agreed to an autopsy.
Autopsy showed (1) acute IMI involving both lungs. Hyphal morphology was consistent with Aspergillus species (septate, narrow-angled, Figure 4). Lung cultures were positive for Aspergillus fumigatus. (2) Acute IMI in both heart ventricles, with wide-angled, aseptate hyphae, consistent with mucormycosis (Figure 5); molecular studies (28 s/internal transcriber sequence (ITS) RNA identification, University of Washington, Seattle) came back positive for Lichtheimia corymbifera. (3) Cervical, mediastinal lymph node, thyroid gland, and left kidney (Figure 5) IMI. (4) Cerebral abscesses of the left temporal and parietal lobes with fungal organisms in the blood vessels and brain parenchyma, consistent with mucorales (Figure 6), and filamentous organisms identified with GMS/FITE stains, consistent with Nocardia (Figure 7).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 79-year-old man with chronic lymphocytic leukemia presented with acute dysphasia and slurred speech after his first cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab, followed 2 months later by multiorgan failure.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One year after being diagnosed with CLL, the patient started chlorambucil and obinutuzumab for fatigue and progressive anemia (Hb 8.9 g/dL) and presented after cycle 1 with slurred speech/dysphasia, three left temporoparietal brain abscesses, and a pulmonary nodule diagnosed by plasma cell-free DNA NGS as disseminated Nocardia abscessus. Treated with high-dose dexamethasone (4 mg qid tapered over 6 weeks) plus ceftriaxone, minocycline, and linezolid, his dysphasia and cerebral edema recurred upon stopping dexamethasone at week 6, prompting re-initiation of dexamethasone (4 mg bid). Two weeks later (2 months after initial presentation), he was admitted to the ICU in fulminant respiratory, renal, and cardiac failure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (diagnosed 1 year prior; treated with 1 cycle of chlorambucil and obinutuzumab); hypertension; retired construction worker and active avid gardener; no prior corticosteroid use before brain abscess presentation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive initially for baseline fatigue and acute dysphasia/slurred speech, followed at 2 months by multiorgan failure.

objective.physical_examination: Initial physical exam was normal except for dysphasia/slurred speech. At 2 months, he presented in acute respiratory, renal, and cardiac failure.
objective.routine_investigations: Pre-chemotherapy baseline labs: hemoglobin 8.9 g/dL, ANC 2.7 x 10^9/L, ALC 16.3 x 10^9/L, AMC 0.3 x 10^9/L, and IgG 805 mg/dL. Initial blood cultures and serum cryptococcal antigen were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial brain MRI showed three left temporal and parietal lobe abscesses with marked edema and chest CT showed a pulmonary nodule (which cavitated as brain abscesses shrank on anti-nocardial therapy). Initial serum Aspergillus galactomannan and 1,3-beta-D-glucan were negative, and stereotactic brain biopsy missed the necrotic core; however, plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing (cfDNA NGS) detected a strong signal for Nocardia abscessus. At 2-month ICU readmission (after prolonged dexamethasone), brain MRI showed shrinking prior abscesses but numerous new acute cerebral infarcts, chest CT showed multiple new cavitary lung masses/abscesses, and repeat serum Aspergillus galactomannan rose to >9.3 (with negative 1,3-beta-D-glucan). Postmortem autopsy confirmed triple invasive infection: (1) bilateral acute invasive pulmonary aspergillosis with narrow-angle septate hyphae and lung cultures positive for Aspergillus fumigatus; (2) disseminated angioinvasive mucormycosis (broad, wide-angle aseptate hyphae) involving both cardiac ventricles, brain parenchyma/vessels, thyroid, left kidney, and cervical/mediastinal lymph nodes identified by 28S/ITS rRNA sequencing as Lichtheimia corymbifera; and (3) GMS/Fite-positive filamentous Nocardia organisms within the left temporoparietal brain abscesses.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Disseminated pulmonary and cerebral Nocardia abscessus infection (diagnosed noninvasively by plasma cfDNA NGS and confirmed at autopsy) following chlorambucil/obinutuzumab for CLL, complicated after 8 weeks of high-dose dexamethasone by fatal dual invasive mold superinfection with bilateral pulmonary Aspergillus fumigatus (serum galactomannan >9.3, autopsy lung culture) and disseminated cardiac, cerebral, renal, thyroid, and nodal Lichtheimia corymbifera mucormycosis (confirmed by autopsy histopathology and 28S/ITS molecular sequencing). The patient died in the ICU after transition to comfort measures.
